`npm run check:decisions` fails while any entry is still `open`. Resolve one by

auth_redirect_urls.question: What origin do the authentication emails send a real user to?
why: Read from the live project on 2026-08-05: site_url is http://localhost:5173 and
uri_allow_list is http://localhost:5173/**. Every link GoTrue generates — signup
confirmation, password reset, email-change confirmation — resolves against a
developer's machine.
This became load-bearing the moment mailer_autoconfirm was turned OFF (also
2026-08-05, closing the account-squatting hole). Confirmation is now REQUIRED, so
the first real account cannot be completed at all, and no password can be reset.
The app asks for the right thing — resetPasswordForEmail passes redirectTo:
window.location.origin — but GoTrue validates that against uri_allow_list and
silently FALLS BACK to site_url when it does not match. So there is no open
redirect here; there is a silent one. Nothing in the app, the build, the five
suites or CI can observe a dashboard setting, which is why this is a gate and not
a note.
Listing localhost as a permitted callback also means any process on that port on a
user's machine is a valid recipient of an auth token fragment.
This is NOT a second static-host decision — it is the half of that decision that
lives outside the repository. legal:release already blocks on the {{FILL}}
placeholders; nothing at all blocks on this, and the two are resolved by different
people in different places on different days. That asymmetry is the whole reason
for the entry.
howToResolve: Answer the static-host question first (DECISIONS-AND-ASSESSMENTS.md s.7) — this is
downstream of it and cannot be settled before it.
Then, in the Supabase dashboard: Authentication -> URL Configuration. Set Site URL
to that https:// origin and replace the allow list with '<origin>/**'. Keep
http://localhost:5173/** only if local development against PRODUCTION auth is
genuinely wanted; preferring a separate dev project is the safer answer and closes
the token-to-localhost path.
Verify with: curl https://dhxsamkaqszffajcwuzn.supabase.co/auth/v1/settings and a
real password-reset mail to yourself — the link must land on the deployed app.
Then add it to compliance/verified.json so it is re-checked rather than assumed.

trademark_clearance.outcome: RENAME before launch. The question is answered; the rename itself is NOT done — the app, the documents and the package are all still called FitPulse. This entry records the decision, not its execution: the outstanding work is tracked in LEGAL-LIABILITY-AUDIT.md under 'Rename (trademark_clearance)', which lists every hard-coded occurrence. Do not read a green check:decisions as 'the name is settled'. Launch is blocked independently by legal:release while the static host is unchosen, so the two cannot silently diverge before a deploy.
trademark_clearance.evidence: LEGAL-LIABILITY-AUDIT.md § 'Rename (trademark_clearance)'. Search evidence gathered 2026-08-05: beyond the App Store and Google Play listings already recorded below, https://fitpulse.jp ships a free iOS workout tracker that logs strength and cardio and 'visualises muscle engagement' to 'reveal imbalances' — the same name, the same Nice class and a feature set matching this app's muscle donut. That is the strongest form of prior use short of a registration. The EUIPO/UKIPO/USPTO register searches were NOT completed (Justia returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches and the registers are not indexed by web search); they were not needed, because prior use this close settles the decision on its own and the answer is to rename either way.
trademark_clearance.question: Is the name FitPulse available to use, and are we prepared to defend it?
why: The name is already in live use by several fitness apps in the identical trademark
class — an App Store 'FitPulse Smart Workout Planner', a Google Play 'FitPulse: Gym
Fitness Planner', fitpulse.ai, and others. Prior use in the same field supports a
passing-off claim in the UK/EU and a Lanham Act s.43(a) claim in the US without
anyone holding a registration; a registration makes it straightforward.
The realistic loss is not damages — it is the store listing or the domain, removed
on a complaint at whatever moment the app finally has users. Renaming before launch
costs a day. Renaming after costs the brand, the domain and every link to it.
howToResolve: Search EUIPO (euipo.europa.eu), UKIPO and USPTO TESS for 'FitPulse' and near marks
in Nice classes 9, 41 and 42. Then choose: proceed, rename, or proceed knowingly.
If the answer is 'proceed', re-read TERMS.md s.6.2 — it must not claim ownership of
branding we do not own.

uk_gdpr_representative.outcome: ACCEPT THE RISK KNOWINGLY. No UK Art. 27 representative is appointed, UK signup is not geo-blocked, and TERMS.md Schedule B.2 continues to hold the service out to UK consumers. This is a deliberate, informed choice re-taken on 2026-08-05 with Schedule B.2 expressly weighed and with Art. 83(2)(b) understood — an intentional infringement is an aggravating factor, and this record is itself evidence the breach is knowing. That was accepted as the price of not paying for a representative on a pre-launch personal project with no users. Revisit before any real user acquisition: the exposure scales with UK users, and appointing a representative later does not cure the period without one.
uk_gdpr_representative.evidence: compliance/DECISIONS-AND-ASSESSMENTS.md section 3, updated 2026-08-05 to record this as re-taken with Schedule B.2 in view rather than before it
uk_gdpr_representative.question: Do we appoint a UK GDPR Art. 27 representative, or stop serving UK users?
why: Establishment in Latvia settles Art. 27 for the EEA and does nothing for the UK.
The Art. 27(2) occasional-processing exemption is unavailable because this is health
data. So serving UK users without a representative is a UK GDPR infringement in its
own right, enforceable by the ICO.
What makes it sharper than incidental reach: TERMS.md Schedule B.2 actively holds the
service out to UK consumers, with a Consumer Rights Act section, UK courts and a UK
complaints route. We are not accidentally reachable from the UK; the documents target
it.
DECISIONS-AND-ASSESSMENTS.md section 3 already records a decision to accept this. That
entry is a good record and it does not close this gate on its own, because it was
taken before Schedule B.2 was weighed and because Art. 83(2)(b) treats an intentional
infringement as an aggravating factor — the record proves the breach was knowing.
howToResolve: Either appoint a UK representative (roughly EUR 100-500/yr) and name them in
PRIVACY.md s.1 alongside the controller, or geo-block UK signup AND delete Schedule
B.2 from TERMS.md. Holding the service out to a market you have decided not to serve
lawfully is the worst of the three options.

image_rights.outcome: DROP THE PHOTOGRAPHS ENTIRELY — done, not merely decided. All four day-tile images were deleted from Assets/, their imports removed from src/, and SessionType's img/pos fields plus the tile markup's branch removed with them, so the app now ships no third-party imagery at all and the personality-rights category is closed rather than mitigated. Verification done first and it changed the picture: all four Pexels IDs were re-opened and confirmed live under the licence, and the images themselves were inspected — only 5327522 (push) and 5799855 (legs) show an identifiable face, 34043598 (pull) is a pure back view and 8544616 (custom) is capped with the face shadowed. Assets/CREDITS.md had recorded 'Yes' for all four and is now corrected. NOTE: this answer is correct for NO images. Adding any image back makes it stale — re-open this entry in the same change, because check:decisions cannot detect that on its own.
image_rights.evidence: Assets/CREDITS.md — kept as the provenance record now that the files are gone; carries the confirmed photo IDs, the per-image identifiability assessment and the 2026-08-05 checked dates
image_rights.question: Do we keep stock photographs of identifiable people in a health product?
why: The four day-tile images are Pexels photographs of identifiable people, used to
illustrate a health and fitness product. Pexels does not obtain or supply model
releases, and health/fitness use is the standard carve-out in stock licences because
it implies endorsement. That engages personality rights in the EU and right of
publicity / false endorsement in the US.
Assets/CREDITS.md records what is used and the checklist to work through. The photo
IDs there are reconstructed from filenames and have not been re-opened and confirmed.
howToResolve: Verify each photo ID still resolves under the Pexels licence and fill in the
'checked' column in Assets/CREDITS.md. Then decide deliberately whether to keep
identifiable faces or swap to images where no one is recognisable — for tiles showing
equipment and movement that costs nothing visually and removes the category.
